question: The names the PostgreSQL manual itself uses, with a definition and the version they apply to: MVCC, snapshot, row version (tuple), xmin / xmax, transaction ID (XID) and its size, how XIDs compare (circular, modulo 2^32), epoch or 64-bit form if the manual names one, frozen XID and freezing, relfrozenxid / datfrozenxid, MultiXact ID and relminmxid / datminmxid, the visibility map bits, dead tuple, aggressive vacuum, the autovacuum run "to prevent wraparound", and the failsafe. Must find: one Rank 1 or 3 source per term, so later workers search for the right words.

sources.rank_basis: tier A: github.com/postgres/ (source code at release tag REL_19_0)
tier A: github.com/postgres/ (source code at release tag REL_19_0)

facts.summary: The PostgreSQL 19 manual says an UPDATE or DELETE leaves the old row version in place, because multiversion concurrency control (MVCC) needs it while other transactions may still see it.
facts.quote: In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE or DELETE of a row does not immediately remove the old version of the row. This approach is necessary to gain the benefits of multiversion concurrency control (MVCC, see Chapter 13): the row version must not be deleted while it is still potentially visible to other transactions.

facts.summary: The manual's name for row versions no transaction needs is "dead row versions"; standard VACUUM removes them and marks the space reusable.
facts.quote: The standard form of VACUUM removes dead row versions in tables and indexes and marks the space available for future reuse.

facts.summary: Transaction IDs (XIDs) are 32 bits; past about 4 billion transactions the XID counter wraps around to zero, which the manual calls transaction ID wraparound.
facts.quote: But since transaction IDs have limited size (32 bits) a cluster that runs for a long time (more than 4 billion transactions) would suffer transaction ID wraparound: the XID counter wraps around to zero, and all of a sudden transactions that were in the past appear to be in the future

facts.summary: Normal XIDs compare by modulo 2^32 arithmetic (the saved text shows the superscript as "232"), so the normal XID space is circular, with two billion older and two billion newer XIDs for each one.
facts.quote: Normal XIDs are compared using modulo-232 arithmetic. This means that for every normal XID, there are two billion XIDs that are … another way to say it is that the normal XID space is circular with no endpoint.

facts.summary: VACUUM marks rows as frozen: inserted by a transaction old enough that its effects are visible to all current and future transactions.
facts.quote: VACUUM will mark rows as frozen, indicating that they were inserted by a transaction that committed sufficiently far in the past that the effects of the inserting transaction are certain to be visible to all current and future transactions.

facts.summary: FrozenTransactionId is a reserved XID outside the normal comparison rules, always older than every normal XID; frozen row versions are treated as if inserted by it.
facts.quote: PostgreSQL reserves a special XID, FrozenTransactionId, which does not follow the normal XID comparison rules and is always considered older than every normal XID. Frozen row versions are treated as if the inserting XID were FrozenTransactionId

facts.summary: Before 9.4, freezing overwrote the row's insertion XID in the xmin system column with FrozenTransactionId; from 9.4 on it sets a flag bit and keeps the original xmin.
facts.quote: In PostgreSQL versions before 9.4, freezing was implemented by actually replacing a row's insertion XID with FrozenTransactionId, which was visible in the row's xmin system column. Newer versions just set a flag bit, preserving the row's original xmin for possible forensic use.

facts.summary: Exact reserved XID values: FrozenTransactionId is 2 and BootstrapTransactionId is 1; both are treated as older than every normal XID.
facts.quote: rows with xmin equal to FrozenTransactionId (2) may still be found in databases pg_upgrade'd from pre-9.4 versions. … system catalogs may contain rows with xmin equal to BootstrapTransactionId (1), indicating that they were inserted during the first phase of initdb. Like FrozenTransactionId, this special XID is treated as older than every normal XID.

facts.summary: An aggressive vacuum freezes all eligible unfrozen XID and MXID values, including those on pages that are all-visible but not all-frozen, which normal VACUUMs may skip.
facts.quote: Therefore, normal VACUUMs won't always freeze every old row version in the table. When that happens, VACUUM will eventually need to perform an aggressive vacuum, which will freeze all eligible unfrozen XID and MXID values, including those from all-visible but not all-frozen pages.

facts.summary: The manual uses the name "anti-wraparound autovacuum" for the autovacuum triggered when a table reaches autovacuum_freeze_max_age.
facts.quote: A value higher than autovacuum_freeze_max_age wouldn't make sense because an anti-wraparound autovacuum would be triggered at that point anyway

facts.summary: relfrozenxid (in pg_class) holds the oldest unfrozen XID left at the end of the last VACUUM that advanced it, typically the last aggressive VACUUM.
facts.quote: the relfrozenxid column of a table's pg_class row contains the oldest remaining unfrozen XID at the end of the most recent VACUUM that successfully advanced relfrozenxid (typically the most recent aggressive VACUUM).

facts.summary: datfrozenxid (in pg_database) is a lower bound on the database's unfrozen XIDs, the minimum of its tables' relfrozenxid values.
facts.quote: the datfrozenxid column of a database's pg_database row is a lower bound on the unfrozen XIDs appearing in that database … it is just the minimum of the per-table relfrozenxid values within the database.

facts.summary: In the recovery steps the page names a column "relminxid"; the rest of the page names only relfrozenxid and relminmxid.
facts.quote: it is also possible to issue manual VACUUM commands on the tables where relminxid is oldest.

facts.summary: A multixact ID encodes lock information when more than one transaction locks a row at once, because the tuple header has little room for it.
facts.quote: Multixact IDs are used to support row locking by multiple transactions. Since there is only limited space in a tuple header to store lock information, that information is encoded as a … or multixact ID for short, whenever there is more than one transaction concurrently locking a row.

facts.summary: The multixact ID sits in the tuple header's xmax field, its members are stored in pg_multixact, and multixact IDs are a 32-bit counter like XIDs.
facts.quote: Information about which transaction IDs are included in any particular multixact ID is stored separately in the pg_multixact subdirectory, and only the multixact ID appears in the xmax field in the tuple header. Like transaction IDs, multixact IDs are implemented as a 32-bit counter and corresponding storage

facts.summary: pg_class.relminmxid stores the oldest multixact ID that may still appear in a table; when older than vacuum_multixact_freeze_table_age, an aggressive vacuum is forced.
facts.quote: For each table, pg_class.relminmxid stores the oldest possible multixact ID still appearing in any tuple of that table. If this value is older than vacuum_multixact_freeze_table_age, an aggressive vacuum is forced.

facts.summary: An autovacuum running to prevent transaction ID wraparound shows "(to prevent wraparound)" at the end of its pg_stat_activity query, or started_by = autovacuum_wraparound in pg_stat_progress_vacuum, and is not automatically interrupted.
facts.quote: if the autovacuum is running to prevent transaction ID wraparound (i.e., the autovacuum query name in the pg_stat_activity view ends with (to prevent wraparound) or the started_by column in the pg_stat_progress_vacuum view shows autovacuum_wraparound value), the autovacuum is not automatically interrupted.

facts.summary: This page names the failsafe threshold vacuum_failsafe_age (and vacuum_multixact_failsafe_age) only in autovacuum prioritization, without defining the failsafe itself.
facts.quote: The transaction ID component measures the age in transactions of the table's pg_class.relfrozenxid field as compared to autovacuum_freeze_max_age. Furthermore, this component increases greatly once the age surpasses vacuum_failsafe_age.

facts.summary: Vacuum keeps a visibility map per table recording which pages hold only tuples known visible to all active and future transactions.
facts.quote: Vacuum maintains a visibility map for each table to keep track of which pages contain only tuples that are known to be visible to all active transactions (and all future transactions, until the page is again modified).

facts.summary: The PostgreSQL 19 glossary spells it "Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC)": PostgreSQL makes new versions of tuples on change and must remove old versions once no transaction can see them.
facts.quote: A mechanism designed to allow several transactions to be reading and writing the same rows without one process causing other processes to stall. In PostgreSQL, MVCC is implemented by creating copies (versions) of tuples as they are modified; after transactions that can see the old versions terminate, those old versions need to be removed.

facts.summary: A tuple is an ordered collection of attributes; a tuple in a table is often called a row (the glossary entry "Row" points to "Tuple").
facts.quote: A collection of attributes in a fixed order. That order may be defined by the table (or other relation) where the tuple is contained, in which case the tuple is often called a row.

facts.summary: A transaction ID, abbreviated xid, is the sequential identifier a transaction gets when it first modifies the database.
facts.quote: The numerical, unique, sequentially-assigned identifier that each transaction receives when it first causes a database modification. Frequently abbreviated as xid.

facts.summary: On disk an xid is 32 bits, so about four billion write XIDs exist; a 32-bit epoch extends that.
facts.quote: When stored on disk, xids are only 32-bits wide, so only approximately four billion write transaction IDs can be generated; to permit the system to run for longer than that, epochs are used, also 32 bits wide.

facts.summary: At the maximum xid value the counter starts over at 3, since lower values are reserved, and the epoch goes up by one.
facts.quote: When the counter reaches the maximum xid value, it starts over at 3 (values under that are reserved) and the epoch value is incremented by one.

facts.summary: The manual names a 64-bit form: epoch and xid taken together, with details in Section 67.1 of the version 19 manual.
facts.quote: In some contexts, the epoch and xid values are considered together as a single 64-bit value; see Section 67.1 for more details.

facts.summary: Each page's visibility map entry has two bits: all-visible (every tuple visible to all transactions) and all-frozen (every tuple marked frozen).
facts.quote: The visibility map entry for each page stores two bits: the first one (all-visible) indicates that all tuples in the page are visible to all transactions. The second one (all-frozen) indicates that all tuples in the page are marked frozen.

facts.summary: Vacuum is the removal of outdated tuple versions plus related MVCC processing, run by the VACUUM command or by autovacuum.
facts.quote: The process of removing outdated tuple versions from tables or materialized views, and other closely related processing required by PostgreSQL's implementation of MVCC.

facts.summary: Bloat is data-page space that holds no current row versions, such as free space or outdated row versions.
facts.quote: Space in data pages which does not contain current row versions, such as unused (free) space or outdated row versions.

facts.summary: The source at tag REL_19_0 uses one SnapshotData struct for both regular MVCC snapshots and special snapshots with non-MVCC semantics.
facts.quote: We use SnapshotData structures to represent both "regular" (MVCC) snapshots and "special" snapshots that have non-MVCC semantics.

facts.summary: Under an MVCC snapshot a tuple is visible only if valid for that snapshot: it excludes transactions in progress at the snapshot, those started after it, and the current command's changes.
facts.quote: A tuple is visible iff the tuple is valid for the given MVCC snapshot. … Does _not_ include: … transactions shown as in-progress by the snapshot … transactions started after the snapshot was taken

facts.summary: An MVCC snapshot never sees XIDs at or above its xmax and sees older XIDs except those it lists as in progress.
facts.quote: An MVCC snapshot can never see the effects of XIDs >= xmax. It can see the effects of all older XIDs except those listed in the snapshot.

facts.summary: A snapshot has its own xmin and xmax fields (XIDs below xmin visible, at or above xmax invisible), distinct from a tuple's xmin and xmax.
facts.quote: TransactionId xmin;			/* all XID < xmin are visible to me */ TransactionId xmax;			/* all XID >= xmax are invisible to me */

facts.summary: For a normal MVCC snapshot, the xip array lists the transaction IDs in progress when it was taken (empty if taken during recovery).
facts.quote: For normal MVCC snapshot this contains the all xact IDs that are in progress, unless the snapshot was taken during recovery in which case it's empty.

facts.summary: In the REL_19_0 source, heap VACUUM has three phases; phase I prunes and freezes tuples and saves dead tuples' TIDs.
facts.quote: Heap relations are vacuumed in three main phases. In phase I, vacuum scans relation pages, pruning and freezing tuples and saving dead tuples' TIDs in a TID store.

facts.summary: The source calls it VACUUM's "failsafe mechanism", which exists to avoid transaction ID wraparound; once it triggers, vacuum may skip phases II and III.
facts.quote: If phase I identified very few dead index entries or if vacuum's failsafe mechanism has triggered (to avoid transaction ID wraparound), vacuum may skip phases II and III.

facts.summary: Vacuums are aggressive or normal; an aggressive one must scan every unfrozen tuple to advance relfrozenxid and avoid wraparound.
facts.quote: Vacuums are either aggressive or normal. Aggressive vacuums must scan every unfrozen tuple in order to advance relfrozenxid and avoid transaction ID wraparound.

facts.summary: The failsafe triggers when relfrozenxid and/or relminmxid is dangerously far in the past; it makes VACUUM skip further index vacuuming, heap vacuuming and truncation.
facts.quote: Trigger the failsafe to avoid wraparound failure when vacrel table has a relfrozenxid and/or relminmxid that is dangerously far in the past. Triggering the failsafe makes the ongoing VACUUM bypass any further index vacuuming and heap vacuuming. Truncating the heap is also bypassed.

facts.summary: When the failsafe triggers, VACUUM stops applying any cost-based delay it started with.
facts.quote: Any remaining work (work that VACUUM cannot just bypass) is typically sped up when the failsafe triggers. VACUUM stops applying any cost-based delay that it started out with.

facts.summary: The failsafe logs a WARNING naming the table, with the detail that its relfrozenxid or relminmxid is too far in the past.
facts.quote: bypassing nonessential maintenance of table … as a failsafe after %d index scans … The table's relfrozenxid or relminmxid is too far in the past.

facts.summary: Exact value: VACUUM runs a failsafe check each time it scans another 4GB of pages.
facts.quote: Perform a failsafe check each time we scan another 4GB of pages.

conflicts.topic: where the XID counter restarts when it wraps
conflicts.note: Routine Vacuuming says the XID counter wraps around to zero; the Glossary says it starts over at 3, since lower values are reserved (both PostgreSQL 19 manual pages)
